The best free colour palette and contrast tools

A palette tool should find colours in a picture, make harmonies from one colour, check that text stays readable and hand the palette to your design or code tools. Here is what each offers, from its own pages.

We make Colours, one of the tools on this page. Every fact about the other tools comes from their own pages, linked under each one, as they read on 2026-10-25. Prices and features change: check each site before you choose.

How we compared them

  • Free, and what an account or plan adds
  • Colours from a picture
  • Harmonies and scales from one colour
  • WCAG contrast check
  • Export files (CSS, Tailwind, ASE, GPL)

1. Colours (ours)

Best for: Picking colours from your own pictures privately, checking contrast and exporting a palette as code or a swatch file in one page.

Good

  • Pictures are read in the browser, never uploaded
  • CSS variables, Tailwind config, JSON, Adobe .ase and GIMP .gpl exports, and those files open again
  • HEX, RGB, HSL, OKLCH and CMYK, with out-of-gamut OKLCH mapped into sRGB

Not so good

  • No library of shared palettes to browse
  • No colour blindness preview
  • No PDF or image export of the palette

Open Colours

2. Coolors

Best for: Generating and browsing palettes fast, with a large library and plugins for design tools.

Good

  • Spacebar generator and over 10 million palettes to explore
  • Exports to PDF, image, CSS, ASE, SVG, code and Tailwind
  • Palette Visualizer previews colours on designs

Not so good

  • The free plan keeps up to 10 palettes; its page lists Image Picker colour extraction and advanced export among the Pro features

Coolors website · Sources: Coolors home page

3. Adobe Color

Best for: Designers in Adobe apps who want harmony rules on a colour wheel and palettes saved to their library.

Good

  • Monochromatic, complementary, analogous, triadic and split-complementary rules on a colour wheel
  • Colour blindness preview
  • Saves palettes to your library for other projects

Not so good

  • Its colour wheel page does not mention export files

Adobe Color website · Sources: Adobe Color, color wheel

4. WebAIM Contrast Checker

Best for: Checking one text and background pair against WCAG, with a link to share the result.

Good

  • Lightness sliders to adjust either colour
  • Permalink and a JSON API for the result
  • Alpha for the foreground

Not so good

  • Checks one pair; it does not make or export palettes

WebAIM Contrast Checker website · Sources: WebAIM Contrast Checker

Which one to choose

Colours is our pick when the colours come from your own pictures and the palette has to end up in code or a design tool: the eyedropper, the main colours, the contrast check and the exports are on one page, and nothing is uploaded.

Choose Coolors for its generator, library and plugins, Adobe Color for its colour wheel and Adobe library, and the WebAIM checker to check and share a single pair.

Questions

Which contrast ratio do I need?

WCAG AA asks for 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text and UI parts; AAA asks for 7:1 and 4.5:1. All four tools show the ratio.

Which file opens in Photoshop or Illustrator?

An Adobe Swatch Exchange (.ase) file. Colours and Coolors both export one.

Is my picture uploaded?

Not in Colours: it is read in your browser. Check each other tool's own privacy notes.
